hook.text: Fly over Kansas and you'll see green circles from the air—each one a center pivot irrigation system.

buildup.text: A long pipe on wheels rotates around a central well, spraying water in a quarter-mile circle.

discovery.text: Center pivots turned the semi-arid Great Plains into one of the world's most productive farming regions.

twist.text: Most pivots pump from the Ogallala Aquifer, which is being drained far faster than rainfall recharges it.

climax.text: When the aquifer runs dry—projected in parts within decades—those green circles will turn brown.

punchline.text: The circles are green today. The water won't last forever.

quiz.question: Why are center pivot irrigation fields circular?
options: The pipe rotates around a central well, naturally creating a circle

details.summary: Center pivot irrigation systems rotate a long sprinkler arm around a central point, creating the circular crop patterns visible from aircraft. This topic covers how pivots work, their efficiency compared to flood irrigation, and their dominance in large-scale farming.
details.whyItMatters: Center pivots irrigate more farmland worldwide than any other sprinkler type. They transformed arid regions like the US Great Plains into productive cropland by making groundwater accessible efficiently.
takeaways: A single center pivot can irrigate a 130-acre circle from one water source
Pivots use 20–30% less water than flood irrigation through targeted sprinkler delivery
Low-pressure drop nozzles near the ground reduce evaporation and wind drift significantly

faq.question: How does a center pivot irrigation system work?
faq.answer: A long pipe mounted on wheeled towers rotates around a central well pump. Sprinklers along the pipe distribute water as the system slowly circles the field, typically completing one rotation every 1–3 days depending on crop water needs.

faq.question: Why are center pivots so widely used in agriculture?
faq.answer: Pivots are relatively simple, require minimal labor once installed, cover large areas efficiently, can be automated with timers and sensors, and apply water more uniformly and with less waste than flood or furrow irrigation methods.
